title: Particle-model figures ask: does the stochastic model conserve what it must, and does it add the spread that the deterministic model lacks?
summary: Stochastic closures replace a single deterministic value with a distribution sampled by particles. The reading skill is to check first what the model must conserve (mean, energy balance), then what it is meant to add (spread, off-manifold scatter, backscatter), and to ask whether the sampling error is small enough to see the difference.

media.alt: A grid of panels titled Mixing Model Comparison, bimodal initial condition, N equals 600. Top left: scalar variance against time times mixing rate on a log axis, with three model curves overlapping, falling from about 0.25 to about 0.0006 and then jumping back to 0.25 at times 1 and 2. Top right: the mean stays at 0.5. Below: histograms of the scalar for three models at times 0, 1 and 3; the time 1 and time 3 histograms look identical, with a central spike at 0.5 and remnants at 0 and 1.

source.caption: Mixing-model comparison
source.note: Group: a three-model mixing comparison (IEM, CURL, EMST) on a two-peak scalar distribution; a Monte Carlo variance-reduction comparison; a temperature against mixture-fraction scatter for the three mixing models; a stochastic velocity model comparison (SLM against GLM) and a stochastic Smagorinsky sub-grid model. These are method-demonstration figures, not validated against experiment.

read_the_figure.question: Does each stochastic model conserve what it should, and what extra statistical behaviour does it produce compared with the simple one?
read_the_figure.axes: Mixing: scalar variance against dimensionless time (log y), mean against time, and histograms of the scalar phi at times 0, 1 and 3. Variance reduction: RMS error against sample size on log-log axes, and a bar chart of speed-up. Scatter: temperature against mixture fraction, coloured by phi. Velocity models: kinetic energy, Reynolds-stress components and anisotropy against time. SGS: histograms of eddy viscosity, viscosity against strain rate, backscatter probability against spread, and the energy spectrum E(k) against wavenumber.
look_at: Start with the conserved quantity. In the mixing figure the mean must stay at 0.5 for every model: the straight line in the top-right panel does so. In the velocity figure the kinetic energy must follow the imposed dissipation.

Then the thing the model is meant to change. Variance decay rate for mixing models; scatter around a manifold for the T-xi plot; anisotropy for the velocity models; sign and spread of eddy viscosity for the SGS model.
Check each curve against a reference line on the same panel. The black dashed line in the variance panel is the theoretical IEM decay exp(-2 Omega t).
Look at the sample size. N = 600 particles in the mixing figure and N = 800 in the velocity figure: histograms and ratios then have visible noise.
For the variance-reduction figure, read the left panel as the evidence and the right panel as a claim that the left must support. A speed-up of 40 should be derivable from the left curves.
In the SGS spectrum, look at what happens beyond the cutoff wavenumber (dotted line) for the reference, the deterministic model and the stochastic model.
read_the_figure.proves: These figures can show that a particle model reproduces known limits (mean conservation, an analytic decay law, constant-dissipation energy decay) and that it adds a certain kind of spread. They cannot show that a closure is accurate for a real flow; that needs a comparison with data or a resolved simulation.
if_wrong: Variance that jumps back to its initial value, or histograms at different times that are identical: the particle ensemble has been re-initialised, or a plotted array is not being updated.
A decay faster than the theoretical law with no extra mechanism: a time-step or rate-scaling error.
Temperature values below zero kelvin: unphysical points of a state-space plot, from particles with mixture fraction outside 0 to 1.
A speed-up bar that cannot be derived from the error curves: a hard-coded or nominal value.
Energy that reaches zero at a time different from k0 divided by the dissipation rate when the dissipation is a constant.
must_check: Number of particles, time step and random seed stated.
Conserved quantities plotted and shown to be conserved.
Reference or analytic curve on the same axes.
For Monte Carlo efficiency: repeated runs, so that the error curve is an average and not one realisation.
State-space plots limited to physically valid values.
Axis scales of diagnostic panels appropriate (a panel with values near 1e-17 is round-off).
as_drawn: Values are read off the plots by eye (about 10 percent).

Mixing: the variance falls from about 0.25 to about 0.0006 in one mixing time (the IEM theory line reaches only about 0.034 at that time and about 0.0006 at three mixing times) and then jumps back to 0.25 at t Omega = 1 and again at 2. The three model curves overlap. The histograms at t = 1 and t = 3 are visually identical, each with a spike near 0.5 and remnants near 0 and 1. The subtitle claims EMST is slowest.

Variance reduction: the task is the mean of U squared for uniform U, the exact value 1/3. At N = 100 standard MC error is about 0.014; the Sobol curve is about 0.001. The speed-up bars read 1, 4, 20 and 40. The curves are not monotone.
Scatter: the three panels look the same; all particles lie on the dashed parabola whose peak is about 2400 K at xi = 0.5. Points with xi below 0 or above 1 reach about -1000 K.

Velocity: k starts at about 1.4 and jumps to about 1.7 in the first moments, then reaches the floor at about 0.85 for SLM and about 1.25 for GLM. The anisotropy trajectory panel has a vertical axis scale of order 1e-17.

SGS: log10 Cs spread of 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0 gives histograms that pile up at zero with long tails to 0.002, 0.012 and 0.12. The near-backscatter probability rises from about 20 to about 83 percent for spread 0.2 to 1.2. The spectrum panel shows the stochastic model closer to the reference than the deterministic one beyond the cutoff.

terms.meaning: Represent a distribution by many sample points, each evolving by a simple stochastic rule, and compute statistics from the sample.
A rule for how a scalar value in each particle relaxes toward the local mean due to molecular mixing, which is not resolved.
Interaction by exchange with the mean: each particle relaxes toward the ensemble mean at a rate Omega. It preserves the mean and shrinks the variance as exp(-2 Omega t).
A conserved scalar from 0 (pure fuel) to 1 (pure oxidiser) that tracks how much of each stream is present.
The curve of temperature as a function of mixture fraction that a thin flame would follow. Points off the curve represent local departures from it.
Techniques that reduce Monte Carlo error at the same sample size: antithetic pairs, control variates and quasi-random (Sobol) points.
Sub-grid eddies normally drain energy from the resolved flow (positive viscosity). Backscatter is the opposite transfer of energy from small to large scales.
The deterministic eddy-viscosity closure: viscosity proportional to the square of the filter width and to the strain-rate magnitude.

remember: Check the conserved quantity first, then the added behaviour.
Monte Carlo error scales as 1 over the square root of N; quasi-random points do better for smooth integrands in low dimension.
A lognormal distribution has a mean much larger than its median when its spread is large.
If one state variable is computed from another by a function, the points cannot leave that function's curve.
With constant dissipation epsilon, homogeneous decaying turbulence loses kinetic energy linearly: dk/dt = -epsilon.

understand.title: What a mixing model is for
understand.text: The unresolved molecular mixing must be modelled. Each model relaxes particle values toward the mean in a different way, so the models differ in how the whole distribution, and not the mean, evolves. That is why the figure shows histograms, not just the mean.

understand.title: What variance reduction promises
understand.text: Plain Monte Carlo error falls as N to the power -1/2. Antithetic pairs and control variates reduce the variance constant. Quasi-random sequences change the rate. The honest figure shows several repeated runs and derives the speed-up from them.

understand.title: Why a stochastic closure
understand.text: A deterministic eddy viscosity can only remove energy from the resolved scales. A random viscosity with large spread can sometimes be negative or near zero, representing local backscatter. The price is that its mean must still match the deterministic model, or the model changes the average dissipation.

steps.title: IEM variance decay
steps.note: For a bimodal start at 0 and 1 with equal weights the initial variance is 0.25, so after three mixing times it is 0.25 e^{-6} = 6.2e-4, which is the end of the dashed line in the figure.

steps.title: The mean is conserved
steps.note: Every particle relaxes toward the same mean, so the mean cannot change. This is the check shown in the top-right panel.

steps.title: Monte Carlo error
steps.note: For the variance-reduction task, the standard deviation is 0.298, so the typical error at N = 100 is about 0.03 for a mean over many repeated runs.

steps.title: Control variate
steps.note: With the optimal coefficient the variance falls by the factor 1 - rho^2 = 1/16, a variance reduction of 16, computed here for this specific task.

steps.title: Antithetic pairs
steps.note: Per pair of function evaluations, the variance is 8 times smaller than from two independent samples. The figure's bar reads 4.

steps.title: Lognormal eddy viscosity
steps.note: The mean exceeds the median by 2.6 at sigma = 0.3, 45 at 0.6 and about 40000 at 1.0, which explains the histograms piling up at zero with extremely long tails.

steps.title: Energy decay at constant dissipation
steps.note: With epsilon = 1 and k0 near 1.4, k should reach zero near t = 1.4. The figure's two models reach it at about 0.85 and 1.25.

worked.title: How far above its median is the stochastic viscosity?
worked.problem: The stochastic Smagorinsky model draws log10 of the coefficient from a normal distribution with spread sigma. For sigma = 0.6, by what factor does the mean viscosity exceed the median?

solution.text: The viscosity is proportional to Cs squared, so its logarithm has a spread of twice that of ln Cs.
For a lognormal variable the mean over the median is exp of half the variance.

worked.answer: About 45. The mean viscosity is 45 times the typical (median) value, so a stochastic model with this spread must have its median set far below the deterministic value if its mean is to match the deterministic model's. A histogram of nu has most of its weight near zero.

analyze.q: The mixing figure's variance panel jumps back to 0.25 at t Omega = 1 and 2 and the t = 1 and t = 3 histograms look identical. List two ways the plotting or the run could cause this, and the check for each.
analyze.hint: Re-initialisation inside a loop; saving the same array at different times.

analyze.q: In the T-xi scatter, T is computed from xi through the dashed curve. Explain why no mixing model can place particles off the curve in this figure, and what would have to change for the plot to show off-manifold scatter.
analyze.hint: A deterministic map has no freedom.

analyze.q: The SLM curve reaches zero kinetic energy before the GLM curve, though both are said to have the same dissipation epsilon = 1. What does the straight-line estimate k0/epsilon tell you about each?
analyze.hint: Compute k0 divided by epsilon and compare with 0.85 and 1.25.

evaluate.q: The speed-up bar chart says 40 for Sobol points. What would you need to see in the left panel to believe it, and what does the figure actually show?
evaluate.hint: A speed-up is a ratio of sample sizes at equal error, from averaged runs.

evaluate.q: The stochastic SGS spectrum panel shows energy recovered near the cutoff. What additional evidence would you require to call this an improvement over Smagorinsky?
evaluate.hint: A resolved or measured reference at the same Reynolds number, and total dissipation compared.

create: Redraw the variance-reduction figure with 200 repeated runs per sample size, an error band, fitted slopes and speed-ups computed from the fitted curves.
Design a test that checks the stochastic SGS model preserves the mean dissipation of the deterministic model, and state which statistic you would plot.

checks.q: Why must the mean of the scalar be exactly conserved by IEM?
checks.hint: Every particle relaxes toward the same number.
checks.answer: Because each particle's rate of change is proportional to (phi minus the mean), and the average of that over all particles is zero. The mean therefore cannot change; this is a necessary property of any mixing model.

checks.q: A scalar starts at 0 and 1 in equal parts. After three mixing times under IEM with decay exp(-2 Omega t), what is the variance?
Estimate the plain Monte Carlo error of the mean of U squared at N = 400 using the standard deviation 0.298.
checks.hint: s over square root of N.
checks.answer: 0.298/20 = 0.0149, about 0.015, if averaged over many repeats; a single run can be higher or lower.

checks.q: Why is a stochastic SGS model's mean viscosity a more meaningful target to match than its median?
checks.answer: The resolved energy balance depends on the average dissipation, and the mean of a lognormal is dominated by its tail. Matching the mean keeps the average transfer equal to the deterministic model; matching the median would not.

checks.q: How would you build a mixing-model test that distinguishes IEM from a model that preserves the shape of the distribution?
checks.hint: Compare higher moments, not the variance.
checks.answer: Start from a bimodal or uniform distribution, track variance and also skewness and kurtosis or the full histogram against time for both models, and compare with a case where the exact distribution evolution is known.
